title: Golden ticket line
hero: graphite packing conveyor with inspection gate
start: A tabletop packing line about the length of a forearm runs left to right across a pale neutral tabletop. It is a brushed graphite conveyor on four chamfered legs, with a belt of ivory card slats and fine machining marks on the side rails. Neatly wrapped bars in crisp ivory paper ride the belt at even spacing, their folded ends tucked and creased. At the midpoint a small graphite inspection gate arches over the belt with a softly glowing frosted acrylic window, and beside it rests a single acid-lime check stamp on its pad, the only tool for approving each bar. At the right end a shallow frosted glass tray holds a few accepted bars. A folded apron waits on a graphite stool behind. Faint paper dust lines the belt edges.
end: The same conveyor is frozen mid-surge, running far too fast. Wrapped bars crowd the belt edge to edge, ride up onto each other and tumble off both sides, and torn ivory wrappers peel back in curls that flutter above the gate. The inspection gate is buried to its roof in a heap of bars, its frosted window blocked, and the acid-lime stamp has been knocked off its pad and lies tilted on the pile, half covered. The frosted tray at the far end overflows, with bars sliding off it toward the table edge and one caught mid-drop. The apron has slipped off the stool into the spill. Paper shreds, card crumbs and a haze of dust trace the pileup back along the belt to the feed end.
apocalypse: A wide dry valley stretches to a hazy ridge, its floor a cracked riverbed of compacted ivory wrapper paper, layered and bleached like shale. Across it runs the ruin of the packing line, now the size of a viaduct: graphite legs leaning, belt slats snapped and half buried, and the inspection gate standing as a lone arch with its frosted window shattered and silted with paper grit. Mounds of flattened bars form low ridges along the old flow lines, and dried channels wind between them. In the foreground a slim graphite gantry rig on thin rails straddles one short lane of belt. Its lime rollers turn as it lays fresh ivory slats in a clean straight run, and a jointed arm sets a single intact wrapped bar at the start of the rebuilt lane.

title: Frozen clock
hero: graphite-rimmed office wall clock
start: A round office clock the width of a dinner plate stands on a brushed graphite easel at the back of a pale neutral tabletop. Its sandblasted frosted glass face covers a plain ivory dial with tick marks, and its slim graphite hands rest a hair short of the top, the moment just before leaving time. A thin acid-lime second hand is the only part expected to move. In front sits a small graphite desk with a chamfered top holding a neat stack of four ivory task cards squared to the edge and a closed graphite slab of a laptop. A jacket hangs over the chair back, ready to go, and a frosted acrylic desk lamp glows softly. A faint film of dust rests on the clock's machined rim.
end: The same clock and desk are held in a thin rime of frost, as if the room itself has stopped. The acid-lime second hand is stuck mid-sweep just past the top tick, with fine ice crystals bridging it to the dial. Only the task pile has kept going: ivory cards rise from the desk in a leaning tower past the lamp, fresh cards hang mid-air as they drop onto it from above, and a slide of cards has spilled off the right edge, fanning across the floor and banking against the chair legs. The jacket has been dragged half off the chair by a card drift. Frost feathers creep across the frosted glass face, and frozen card fibres glitter across the desk.
apocalypse: A frost-bound plain of packed ivory card flakes, crusted and wind-scoured, stretches under a pale sky to a line of low ice ridges. Rising from it is the clock, now as tall as a water tower, tilted on its snapped graphite easel. Its frosted glass face is cracked in a wide star and packed with snow-like card fibre. The desk below has become a buried plateau, with only its chamfered corner and the lamp's frosted shade breaking the crust. Long drifts of frozen task cards run downwind from it in layered ridges. On the clock rim, a slim graphite climbing rig clamped to the bezel by four spidery legs has fitted a new lime second hand to the hub, and the hand has just moved one tick, shedding a thin curtain of frost.

title: Road not taken
hero: forked card path with briefcase and toolbox
start: A miniature path of pressed ivory card, a hand's width across, runs from the front of a pale neutral tabletop and splits into two lanes at a graphite signpost with two blank arms. At the fork stand a brushed graphite briefcase with chamfered corners and a matte graphite toolbox with a folding lid, set down side by side as if someone paused to choose. Down the left lane sits a tidy stack of ivory report sheets; down the right, a short frosted acrylic workbench holds one half-built ivory card birdhouse. Set into the signpost base is a small acid-lime compass disc whose needle points exactly between the lanes. Fine crease lines mark the card path, and light scuffs dull the briefcase handle.
end: The same fork, now with both lanes choked. On the left, the report sheets have multiplied into a tall stack that has buckled forward, sending sheets sliding back down the path toward the fork. On the right, the workbench is heaped with unfinished card birdhouses, walls half glued and roofs missing, and several are tumbling off its end. The briefcase has burst open and spilled blank folders across the junction, and the toolbox has tipped, scattering small graphite tools into the paper. The signpost leans, and the acid-lime compass needle is caught mid-swing in a blur. The two drifts of debris meet at the fork, and each can be traced back up its own lane. Paper fibres and card dust hang in the air.
apocalypse: A broad valley of layered ivory paper sediment stretches to distant folded card hills, split down the middle by a dry gorge. On either side run the two old paths, now wide roads of cracked card slabs. One is lined with collapsed towers of weathered report sheets like fallen cliffs; the other is scattered with bleached, roofless birdhouse shells the size of barns. At the head of the valley the signpost lies snapped across the gorge, and the briefcase and toolbox sit half buried as grey boulders with their lids jammed open. On the left rim, a slim graphite bridge-laying rig on tracked feet extends a lime truss span over the gorge, and its far end has just touched the right rim, joining the two roads again.

title: Blinking drive
hero: graphite server rack with frosted drive sleds
start: A server rack about the height of a shoebox stands upright near the centre of a pale neutral tabletop. It is a brushed graphite frame with chamfered rails and fine machining marks, holding eight slim drive sleds in two columns, each faced with frosted acrylic. All sit dark except one near the top, where a small acid-lime status light blinks. To the left, a short frosted glass fan housing sits behind a graphite grille; to the right, an ivory card clipboard of blank log sheets lies squared beside a cold mug. A single graphite cable leaves the back of the rack in one tidy curve. A fine layer of dust rests on the top plate, undisturbed.
end: The same rack is overheating. Every sled now glows milky white through its frosted face, and several have been shoved half out of their bays by the heat, with one tipping mid-fall toward the table. The acid-lime light that started it still blinks at the top, now lost in the glare. Heat shimmer rises above the frame, and the hot draught has lifted the log sheets off the clipboard: they curl and flip upward, one airborne above the mug. The fan housing's glass has fogged and its grille has bowed outward. The graphite cable has pulled taut and dragged the clipboard to the table edge. The top plate is dulled and faintly warped, and the dust on it has been blown into streaks pointing away from the rack.
apocalypse: A long, dim underground hall stretches away between rows of squat graphite pillars toward a faint doorway of light at the far end. Its floor is drifted with grey-ivory paper dust, rippled like a cave floor. The rack lies toppled against one pillar at enormous scale, its frame bowed and its drive sleds jutting out like broken shelves, their frosted faces crazed and cold. More sleds lie scattered across the floor in half-buried lines, and the old log sheets have fused into brittle drifts along the walls. Beside the rack, a slim graphite tracked carrier with a lime lift fork has just slid one fresh sled into a straightened bay, and a single lime status light on that sled now glows steady, the only light in the hall.

title: Sponsor clutter
hero: small studio set with two chairs
start: A small studio set about the size of a shoebox diorama sits on a pale neutral tabletop. At the back stands a flat backdrop of ivory card with a soft deckled edge, held by two graphite stands. In front are two low graphite chairs angled toward each other and a small frosted acrylic table between them. On the table lies a single ivory contract sheet, folded once and held by an acid-lime paperclip, the one deal that started it all. To the right, a compact graphite camera on a slim tripod faces the chairs, its frosted glass lens dusty. A folded jacket hangs over one chair. The floor is clean apart from a few faint scuffs.
end: The same set is buried under sponsor products. Blank ivory cartons, frosted glass bottles and graphite tins are stacked on both chairs, crammed onto the table and wedged against the backdrop, which is bowing under dozens of unmarked cards pinned across its face. A leaning tower of cartons on the left chair has given way and is frozen mid-collapse, cartons tumbling onto the table and knocking the contract sideways; the acid-lime paperclip has sprung loose and hangs in the air above the pile. The tripod is half buried and tilted, its lens now pointing at a carton. The jacket is pinned under a crate. Torn packing paper and dust spray out from the collapse toward the camera.
apocalypse: A wide sunken basin, like an old quarry, is filled with rubble of crushed ivory cartons, flattened tins and frosted glass shards packed into terraced layers. Its rim rises to a dusty horizon under a pale sky. Toward the centre, the backdrop now stands as a huge cracked cliff face, still pinned with faded blank cards, and the tripod lies across the basin like a fallen pylon. Only the tops of the two chairs break the rubble, one snapped at the backrest. On the near side, a slim graphite boom crane on a narrow tracked base swings its lime hook out over the nearer chair; it has already cleared that seat down to bare graphite and is lifting away the last carton, leaving one clean chair in the ruin.

title: Jump-to-conclusions mat
hero: spring-loaded memo catapult and pigeonhole wall
start: On a pale neutral tabletop, a spring-loaded memo launcher about the size of a stapler sits in the foreground, a brushed graphite base with a coiled spring, a hinged arm and a flat acid-lime paddle at its tip. One folded ivory memo card rests on the paddle, waiting to be decided. Across the table, a wall of blank frosted acrylic pigeonholes stands in a graphite frame, the slots evenly spaced and softly glowing, each with an unmarked tab. A neat stack of unread memos sits squared beside the launcher, and a cold mug stands to the right. The whole setup suggests every decision will be made by where a card happens to land. A faint dust line runs along the pigeonhole frame.
end: The same launcher has been firing without pause. Its spring is fully sprung, and the acid-lime paddle is caught at the top of its swing with a memo just leaving it. Dozens of memo cards are frozen in flight across the table in scattered arcs, some jammed half into the wrong pigeonholes, others bouncing off the frosted frame and ricocheting back. The pigeonhole wall is overstuffed and leaning, a few slots cracked, cards spraying from the bottom row. The unread stack has been knocked flat and fanned across the tabletop, and the mug has tipped, a trail of spilled cold drink running under the cards. Every arc of flight traces back to the launcher's paddle.
apocalypse: A dry mesa landscape of stacked, weathered memo cards rises in terraces toward a pale horizon, the card layers cracked and curled like sedimentary rock. On the nearest plateau sits the launcher at the size of a siege engine, its graphite arm snapped and its spring dulled grey with dust. Far across a shallow ravine, the pigeonhole wall stands as a crumbling cliff honeycombed with broken frosted cells, many packed with bleached cards. Thousands of stray memos lie in drifts between them. A slim graphite rail sorter on thin legs runs along the ravine floor, its lime guide pins setting out a single straight lane of cards from the launcher's base to one intact pigeonhole, the only sensible route across the ruin.

title: Ticket rail overload
hero: kitchen ticket rail over a pass
start: A short kitchen pass about a forearm wide sits on a pale neutral tabletop: a brushed graphite counter with chamfered edges and fine machining marks. Above it runs a slim graphite ticket rail on two brackets, and a frosted acrylic heat lamp hangs over the counter with a soft internal glow. One small ivory order slip is clipped to the rail by a single acid-lime rail clip, its blank face slightly curled at the bottom. On the counter below sits one ivory card plate, empty and clean. To the right, a stack of clean plates waits beside a folded apron. Faint grease-like smudges and paper lint mark the rail. Everything is orderly and ready for one order.
end: The same rail is overloaded. Order slips crowd along its whole length, overlapping three and four deep, bowing the rail in the middle, and fresh slips are frozen mid-fall as the clips give way. The acid-lime clip holding the first slip has been shoved to the far end and is sliding off. Dropped slips spill across the pass in a curling layer, and under the heat lamp the plates are now stacked high in leaning columns, one column tipping sideways toward the table edge with its top plate caught in the air. The apron is buried under slips. Curled paper edges browned by the lamp's heat and a haze of lint trace the overflow back to the rail.
apocalypse: A wide white drift field of old order slips, compacted and curled like wind-packed snow, rolls away toward a low horizon. Rising from it is the ruin of the kitchen pass, now the length of a street: the graphite counter cracked and tilted, the heat lamp's frosted shade split and half filled with slips, and plate columns standing as leaning, weathered towers. The ticket rail lies sagging across the drifts on its broken brackets. In the foreground, a slim graphite rail-crawler has re-hung a clean straight section of rail on new supports. Its jointed arm lifts slips from the drift one at a time, and a row of lime clips holds them in a neat ordered line along the repaired section.

title: Clock-tower deadline
hero: office tower model with a large clock face
start: A slender office tower model about the height of a wine bottle stands at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop. Its body is matte graphite with fine machined window grooves on every floor, each window a small panel of frosted acrylic glowing softly. Near the top, a round clock face of sandblasted frosted glass over an ivory dial with plain tick marks fills one side. Its graphite hour hand sits near the top, and a single acid-lime minute hand is a few ticks away from meeting it. At the tower's base lies a tidy ivory card forecourt with a small stack of blank folders. Light dust gathers in the window grooves. Everything is still and correct.
end: The same tower, with the acid-lime minute hand frozen one tick from the top. The floors below have filled with unfinished work: ivory sheets press against every frosted window, several panes have popped out, and sheets pour from them in streams down the facade. A cascade from the upper floors is caught mid-fall, sheets fluttering outward, and on the forecourt the folder stack has been buried under a growing drift that spreads toward the table edge. The lowest floor has bulged, its window frame split and a jammed wedge of folders forcing it open. Paper dust hangs in the air around the clock. Every stream can be traced from the clock down the facade to the pile.
apocalypse: A high, snowy mountain ridge of compacted ivory paper stretches along a wide horizon under a cold pale sky. Along it stand the stumps of old graphite towers, and the tallest is the clock tower, now the size of a peak, cracked down its facade with its frosted windows long gone and packed with snow-like paper. Its clock face is split, both hands hanging loose. Glaciers of old sheets flow down from the empty windows into the valley below. On a ledge beside the clock, a slim graphite winch rig bolted to the stonework feeds a lime drive gear into the exposed mechanism, and the gear has just engaged: the loose minute hand has lifted and moved one tick.

title: Airport form loop
hero: departure-gate counter with form slot
start: A departure-gate counter about the size of a toaster sits on a pale neutral tabletop: a brushed graphite desk with chamfered corners and a narrow form slot in its face, backed by a frosted glass gate panel that glows softly. In front, a short queue lane of slim graphite stanchions linked by ivory card ribbon stands empty. On the counter lies one crisp ivory form in a frosted acrylic tray, and beside it an acid-lime approval stamp rests on its pad, unused. To the left, a small graphite suitcase stands upright with a folded coat draped across it, set down by someone waiting. The floor is clean, and a thin line of dust runs along the base of the counter.
end: The same gate, many days later. The ivory form has been rejected again and again: copies stream back out of the counter slot and are caught mid-air, arcing onto a growing heap of returned forms that has buried the tray. The acid-lime stamp still sits on its pad, untouched, now half hidden by paper. Beside the gate, the traveller's belongings have spread into a camp: the suitcase lies open, the coat is spread as a blanket, and a row of cold paper cups, a folded pillow and a stack of empty meal trays climb against the stanchions, which are leaning under the weight. Creased forms, crumbs and dust scatter across the lane, all tracing back to the slot.
apocalypse: A bright, sunlit salt flat of pale compacted forms stretches to a flat horizon, its surface cracked into neat polygons. Standing alone on it is the gate, now the size of a hangar: the graphite counter weathered and bleached, the frosted glass gate panel cracked but still upright. The stanchions have become a row of leaning posts trailing frayed card ribbon, and the traveller's suitcase is a half-buried outcrop, lid open and full of drifted paper. Sun-bleached form copies lie in long wind streaks. A slim graphite gate conveyor on low rollers runs through the old gate, and its lime-edged belt is carrying one ivory form through the rebuilt frame and out the far side for the first time.

title: Supply closet heist
hero: locked graphite supply closet
start: A small supply closet about the height of a shoebox stands upright at the back of a pale neutral tabletop: a matte graphite cabinet with chamfered door edges, a sturdy graphite padlock and fine machining marks on the hinges. Taped to its door with one strip of acid-lime tape is a single ivory request form, blank and slightly curled. Through a narrow frosted glass window in the door, a few neat stacks of ivory paper and a box of pens are softly visible. In the foreground an empty frosted acrylic in-tray waits for the approval to come back. A cold mug sits to the left. Light dust has settled on top of the cabinet.
end: The approval never came, and a plan has taken over the table in front of the same closet. Ivory blueprint sheets are unrolled edge to edge, their curling corners held down by graphite timers with plain dials and a frosted acrylic model of the corridor strung with taut thread lines. More sheets have been added faster than the table can hold, and a roll is caught mid-unfurl off the right edge. The cold mug has been knocked over by a sheet, and the in-tray is buried. On the closet door, the acid-lime tape has peeled halfway and the request form hangs by one corner, swinging. Paper fibres drift in the air above the plans.
apocalypse: A deep canyon has been cut through layered strata of compacted blueprint paper, its walls banded in faded ivory and grey, running toward a hazy gap on the horizon. Scattered along the canyon floor are ruins of the plan: giant graphite timers lying on their sides with cracked faces, and the frosted corridor model broken into glassy blocks strung with snapped threads. At the canyon's end stands the supply closet, now as tall as a cliff, its padlock heavy and dust-coated, its window frosted over. A slim graphite arm rig on three thin legs stands at the door, and its lime key is fully turned in the padlock, the shackle just released, with a thin fall of dust sliding from the opening door.

title: Admin-rights ceiling drop
hero: card reader in a frosted glass room
start: A small bright room of sandblasted frosted glass panels, about the size of a shoebox, sits on a pale neutral tabletop with a graphite ceiling grid of square ivory tiles. At its centre, a single graphite pedestal holds a card reader with an acid-lime slot bezel, the one permission everything is waiting on. Outside the room, on a slim graphite rack to the right, sits a blank ivory access request card in a frosted acrylic sleeve. A few frosted acrylic sensor posts stand in a neat ring around the pedestal. A jacket hangs on the rack's hook. The glass is spotless apart from a faint film of dust along the base. Everything is quiet and sealed.
end: Getting that permission now takes a full operation. Two ceiling tiles have been lifted out and hang tilted in the grid, and a small graphite winch mounted above them lowers the request card on thin graphite cables through the opening, the card frozen mid-descent halfway to the reader. The ring of sensor posts has been nudged: one has toppled and is mid-fall, another leans, and dust and tile fragments rain from the ceiling in a thin curtain along the cable path. The acid-lime slot bezel waits below, still empty. The empty sleeve lies dropped on the floor by the rack, the jacket has slipped off its hook, and every piece of debris traces back up to the open ceiling.
apocalypse: A wide white quarry of shattered ivory ceiling tiles and frosted glass shards spreads to a pale, flat horizon, the fragments settled in sloping terraces. Standing out of it are the tall frosted glass panels of the old room, now cliff-sized, cracked and leaning, their surfaces bleached. The graphite ceiling grid lies collapsed across the quarry like fallen scaffolding, and the sensor posts rise here and there as broken frosted columns. At the centre, the pedestal has become a monolith with a dusty, empty reader. A slim graphite tripod rig with a jointed lime arm stands beside it and is sliding a single blank ivory card into the rebuilt reader slot, one clean permission granted.

title: Paperwork twister
hero: loose form on a desk by an open window
start: A small graphite desk with a chamfered top sits on a pale neutral tabletop beside an open window frame of brushed graphite fitted with a tilted sandblasted frosted glass pane. On the desk lies a neat stack of ivory forms squared to the edge, and on top of it one loose form lifts slightly at its acid-lime corner tab, just caught by a draught. A graphite paperweight sits next to the stack, not on it. To the right, a frosted acrylic in-tray holds more forms, and a jacket hangs over the chair. Fine fibres rise from the lifted corner. The rest of the room is still and orderly.
end: The draught has become a storm through the same window. The loose form with its acid-lime tab is at the top of a spiralling column of paperwork that rises from the desk to the ceiling: sheets from the stack and the in-tray are caught mid-whirl, twisting in a tight funnel, with a trail of forms feeding into its base from the scattered stack. The in-tray has flipped and is airborne, the paperweight has slid to the desk edge, and the chair has rolled back with the jacket flapping off it. The frosted glass pane has swung wide open. Dust and paper fibres swirl around the column, and the whole spiral leans back toward the window.
apocalypse: A vast flattened plain stretches to a low horizon under a clearing sky, its surface combed into long curved streaks of pale forms laid down by the storm, some pressed flat, some curled into ridges. Near the centre, the desk lies overturned at the scale of a bridge, graphite legs pointing up, and the window frame stands alone, cracked and leaning, its frosted pane shattered. Torn forms have piled against it in a tall drift. In the middle distance, a slim graphite collector rig on thin wheels moves across the plain, a lime anemometer spinning calmly on its mast, while its low scoop feeds forms onto a neat squared stack on its back.

title: Deadline asteroid
hero: crumpled card asteroid over a desk calendar
start: A small asteroid about the size of a clenched fist, built from tightly crumpled ivory card with a few graphite grit inclusions, hangs on a slim graphite rod stand above a pale neutral tabletop. Beneath it lies a flat ivory desk calendar with a blank grid of squares and crisp edges, and one square is marked by an acid-lime pin, the deadline. To the left, a small graphite desk lamp with a frosted acrylic shade lights the calendar; to the right, three graphite chairs stand pushed in neatly. The asteroid's creases hold faint dust, and a single crumb of card has fallen onto the calendar, the only hint of what is coming.
end: The asteroid has swelled as the deadline closed in, now as wide as the desk and pressing down on the same calendar, whose pages have split and folded under it. Its graphite rod stand has bent in a shallow arc. Small graphite drills are embedded in its surface at several angles, left running by the desk team, and one is frozen mid-slip out of its bore with a spray of card crumbs. The acid-lime pin has been pushed up through a torn calendar square and is tilting toward the edge. The chairs have been shoved back and one has tipped over, a jacket crumpled beneath it. Card grit and dust drift down from the drill holes onto the lamp shade.
apocalypse: A cratered field of pale compacted card dust stretches to a curved, hazy horizon, its surface pocked with shallow impact bowls rimmed with debris. In the largest crater lies the asteroid, now as big as a hill, cracked across its middle and bristling with old graphite drills snapped off at their bases. The desk calendar is a set of broken ivory slabs radiating out from under it, and the lamp stands on the crater rim, its frosted shade split. A slim graphite drill rig with a lime bit has cut the asteroid cleanly in half along the crack, and a narrow conveyor beside it is stacking the cut blocks into a level plinth where a new blank calendar sheet has been laid.

title: Prototype taken for production
hero: card-and-tape prototype on a stand
start: A rough prototype about the size of a shoebox sits on a slim graphite display stand at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop. It is plainly a mock-up: panels of ivory card scored and folded into a boxy device shape, edges held with frayed paper tape, one flap not quite closed and a doubled crease where the card was bent twice. A single strip of acid-lime tape holds on its front panel. To the left, a cutting mat of pale card and a graphite craft knife lie beside offcuts. To the right, an empty frosted acrylic parts tray waits. Fibres fuzz at the cut edges, and card crumbs dot the stand.
end: The same mock-up is now being treated as the real thing. Graphite parts crates have arrived and stack around the stand, lids open with components spilling out, and a taller graphite display plinth has been built around the prototype, pushing it upward. Ivory launch plans are pinned to a frosted board behind it and are spilling off in a slide of sheets. The weight of a graphite bracket bolted to the card front has caused the panel to sag, and the acid-lime tape is peeling mid-rip as the flap swings loose. The parts tray overflows and a crate is caught mid-topple off the table edge. Offcuts and dust are scattered across the cutting mat.
apocalypse: A dry scrubland of wind-rippled ivory card offcuts rolls toward a distant bluff under a hazy sky. At its centre stands the collapsed prototype, now the size of a building, its card panels slumped and bleached, tape hanging in long weathered strips, and one wall folded flat into the ground. Around it, graphite parts crates lie half buried, some split open and spilling dulled components, and the display plinth leans like a broken monument. Beside the ruin, a slim graphite gantry frame with a lime print head moves along thin rails, and it has already built the lower half of the real device in machined graphite and frosted glass, standing solid next to the fallen card version.

title: Monochrome office
hero: monochrome desk with a single lime pencil cup
start: A small office desk sits at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop, everything around it in shades of grey. The desk is matte graphite with chamfered edges; on it sit a graphite desk phone with its handset squared in the cradle, an ivory card memo stack with crisp edges, and a frosted acrylic lamp with a soft grey glow. The only colour is an acid-lime pencil cup in the front right corner, holding a few graphite pencils. Behind, a graphite chair with a grey jacket over its back is pushed in. The surfaces carry a fine, even dust, and the memos show faint grey fibre. Everything is tidy, flat and repetitive.
end: The same desk, now swallowed by grey repetition. Identical graphite mugs have multiplied in long rows across the desk and onto the floor, and the memo stack has been copied into dozens of identical stacks, leaning into each other and tipping over like dominoes toward the edge. A fine grey dust is falling steadily from above, coating every surface, and it has crept up the sides of the acid-lime pencil cup, graying its lower half. The lamp's glow has dimmed to flat grey. One row of mugs is frozen mid-fall off the desk edge, dust puffing where the first one strikes the floor. The chair has been pushed back by the spreading stacks.
apocalypse: A wide grey ash plain of settled paper dust stretches to a flat horizon, broken by the tops of graphite desks buried in long rows like gravestones. Drifts of identical memo stacks have fused into grey ridges, and fallen mugs lie half buried in patterned lines. At the centre, the original desk rises at the size of a house, its chamfered edge cracked and its lamp shade split. A slim graphite spray rig on a tracked base has cleaned one desk surface down to bare metal, and from its lime nozzle a band of acid-lime colour is spreading across that desktop and down one leg into the ash, the first colour on the plain.

title: Harvest quota
hero: graphite weighing platform with a grain quota
start: A low graphite weighing platform about the size of a dinner plate sits on a pale neutral tabletop, its chamfered deck resting on four slim legs with visible bolts. On it rises a neat conical heap of small ivory paper grain pellets, the season's quota. At its front is a round frosted glass gauge with a plain dial and tick marks, its acid-lime needle sitting exactly at the target mark. Above the platform hangs a small graphite hopper with its gate closed. To the right, a stack of empty ivory card sacks is folded neatly beside a graphite scoop. Fine grain dust has settled around the platform feet.
end: The quota has doubled. The hopper above the same platform has swung open and is emptying a second heavy load in a thick falling column, grains frozen mid-air. The heap has doubled, spreading past the deck edges, and the platform is sagging, two legs splaying and one snapped bolt caught flying off. Grain pours over the edges in steady streams, fanning across the tabletop and burying the folded sacks. The acid-lime needle is pinned hard past the end of the dial, and the frosted glass has cracked. The scoop has been shoved to the table edge by the spill. A haze of grain dust hangs in the air, tracing everything back to the hopper.
apocalypse: A drought-cracked lakebed of hard, pale clay stretches to a shimmering horizon, crossed by fissures filled with old ivory grain. Near the centre lies the weighing platform, now the size of a stadium, collapsed on its splayed legs, its deck tilted and cracked, with the hopper fallen alongside like a toppled silo. The gauge stands upright on its own, cracked and bleached. Ridges of hardened grain run out from the ruin in long spill tongues. A slim graphite bucket conveyor with lime buckets climbs from a small grain store at the lakebed's edge to a newly built small platform, and it is dropping one fair, measured load onto the fresh deck.

title: Citation quota
hero: ticket pad and tally counter on a dashboard shelf
start: A narrow dashboard shelf of brushed graphite, about a forearm long, sits on a pale neutral tabletop behind a sandblasted frosted glass windscreen panel. On the shelf lies a thick pad of blank ivory ticket slips on a graphite clipboard, its top slip crisp and unused, with a slim graphite pen clipped alongside. Next to it stands a small mechanical tally counter with unmarked wheels and an acid-lime plunger button, the quota that has to be met. To the left, a cold paper cup sits in a graphite holder, and a folded cap rests on the shelf. The slips show fine fibre at their perforated edges, and dust lines the windscreen base.
end: The same dashboard is a blizzard of slips. The pad has been torn down to its bare card backing, and dozens of ivory slips are frozen mid-air, flying off the clipboard and sticking to everything: the windscreen, the cup, the cap and the shelf edges. The tally counter's unmarked wheels have become a blur, and the acid-lime plunger is caught pressed halfway down. A trail of torn stubs leads from the clipboard across the shelf. The cup has tipped, spilling cold coffee under the slips. The pen has rolled off the edge and is mid-fall. Perforation fluff and paper dust drift in a thin haze across the windscreen.
apocalypse: A long, straight highway of cracked graphite slabs runs across a flat pale dust plain toward a vanishing point on the horizon. Along both verges, wind has piled faded ticket slips into low drifts that have spilled over the carriageway. Midway along, the dashboard shelf lies across the road at the scale of a bridge span, and the frosted windscreen panel stands cracked and leaning beside it. The tally counter is a squat weathered tower with its wheels jammed. A slim graphite service rig on thin wheels is parked beside the counter, and its jointed arm has pulled a lime reset lever: the counter's wheels have just rolled back to blank, shedding dust.

title: The call you can't leave
hero: graphite phone booth with a receiver off the hook
start: A phone booth about the height of a wine bottle stands on a pale neutral tabletop, framed in matte graphite with chamfered corners and four sandblasted frosted glass panels. Inside, a graphite phone unit is fixed to the back panel, and its receiver hangs off the hook on an acid-lime coiled cord, dangling just above the floor. Outside the booth to the right, a small pale kerb of ivory card runs along the edge, and a graphite briefcase stands beside the door, set down by someone who meant to be quick. A folded jacket rests on the briefcase. Faint dust lies on the booth's roof, and the frosted glass shows light smudges.
end: The same booth is closing in. Its frosted panels have been pushed inward and bowed, cracks spreading from the corners, and the graphite frame has pinched so the booth is visibly narrower than before. Ivory work memos, folders and message slips have been crammed in through the door gap and pack the floor. The acid-lime coiled cord is stretched taut out of the door, pulled straight, holding the receiver in mid-air outside. The briefcase has fallen open, spilling folders onto the kerb, and the jacket has slipped under the drift. Glass dust and paper scraps are frozen mid-fall from the cracked panels, all spreading out from the booth.
apocalypse: A ruined street runs into a shallow, flooded lagoon of milky water, where pale ivory paper sediment has settled in rippled banks along the kerbs. At the water's edge the phone booth stands at the size of a tower, its frosted panels cracked and crumpled inward, its graphite frame twisted. The receiver lies in the shallows far from the booth, still attached by its long faded lime cord. Broken folders and memos have silted up against the frame. A slim graphite cutter rig on four jointed legs stands on the kerb, its lime shears having just snipped the cord free at the booth; the loose end is caught mid-recoil above the water.

title: Hospitality-suite vigil
hero: snack tray and empty client chair
start: A small hotel suite corner about the size of a shoebox diorama sits on a pale neutral tabletop. A low graphite side table holds a round frosted glass tray of neat ivory card canapes, cut in small squares and laid in tidy rows. Across from it stands a single graphite armchair with chamfered arms, empty, and on its seat rests a blank acid-lime place card, reserved for the client. Beside the table, two other chairs have jackets on their backs and a stack of ivory brochures on the floor between them. A frosted acrylic floor lamp glows softly. Fine dust sits along the chair arms.
end: Hours have passed in the same suite. The frosted tray has been emptied and refilled so often that three more trays now stack on the table, their canapes curling, drying and crumbling at the edges, and one tray is sliding off the table corner, a few canapes caught mid-fall. Crumbs and card flakes trail across the floor. The brochure stack has toppled and fanned out toward the empty chair. The acid-lime place card has slid to the front edge of the seat and hangs half over it, the chair still empty. The jackets sag from their chair backs, one on the floor. The lamp glows dimmer through a film of dust.
apocalypse: A dusty basin of fine grey-ivory sediment stretches toward a faint horizon lined with low ridges. In the middle stand the ruins of the suite at vast scale: the side table cracked in half, stacked trays fused into a leaning frosted glass column, and old canapes weathered into pale stones scattered through the dust. The brochures have become layered slabs half sunk in the sediment. The empty armchair lies on its back, one arm snapped. A slim graphite lifting rig with a lime cradle has set the chair upright on clean ground and is lowering a fresh ivory folder onto its seat, so the chair is finally filled.

title: Remote volleyball coworker
hero: plain ivory ball on the chair opposite a home desk
start: A small home desk of matte graphite with chamfered corners sits on a pale neutral tabletop, holding a slim graphite laptop slab, a cold mug and a neat stack of ivory card notes. Across the desk, a second graphite chair faces it, and on that chair sits a plain ivory stress ball about the size of a grapefruit, the only other presence in the room. A single acid-lime sticky note is pressed onto the ball, blank, as if left for it. A frosted acrylic lamp glows on the desk, and a jacket hangs unused on a hook by the door. Dust has gathered on the chair opposite, and the note's edge curls slightly.
end: Isolation has piled up around the same ball. Ivory sticky notes cover the desk, the laptop and the opposite chair in overlapping layers, and fresh notes are frozen mid-air, falling from a toppled stack. The acid-lime note is now half buried among ivory ones stuck all over the ball, which has rolled to the edge of its chair seat and is tipping forward. A trail of notes runs from the desk across the floor toward the door, where the jacket has slipped off its hook. The mug has filled with notes. Paper curls and dust drift in the lamp light, all spreading out from the chair opposite.
apocalypse: A small island of pale ivory sand rises from a wide still sea of milky frosted water, with a thin horizon line and a faint shoreline far away where graphite office towers stand. The island is built from the ruins of the home office: the desk lies half sunk in the sand at the size of a reef, the chair opposite is a weathered frame, and the ivory ball rests at the water's edge, bleached and pitted. Drifts of faded notes cover the dunes. A slim graphite raft-building rig on the shore has lashed desk panels into a flat raft and is raising a lime sail on a thin mast, pointed toward the distant towers.

title: Fifteen-minute escape hatch
hero: small hatch behind a filing cabinet
start: A tall graphite filing cabinet with four chamfered drawers stands at the back of a pale neutral tabletop, pulled slightly away from a frosted glass wall panel. In the gap behind it, a small square hatch about the size of a paperback is set into the wall, its brushed graphite frame screwed in with visible fasteners and its door fitted with a single acid-lime handle. In front of the cabinet sits a graphite desk with a neat ivory in-tray and a jacket hung over the chair. A frosted acrylic lamp glows. Scuff marks on the floor show the cabinet has been moved before. Dust lies thin and even.
end: A queue has formed at the same hatch. The filing cabinet has been shoved sideways, drawers hanging open and spilling folders onto the floor, and a line of graphite office chairs stands in single file leading to the acid-lime handle, each chair holding a jacket and an abandoned in-tray. Tasks have piled up behind the queue: ivory folders stack on the desk until the stack buckles and slides, sheets frozen mid-fall. The hatch door is ajar, a thin draught lifting paper from the nearest chair. Scuff marks and dropped sheets trace the queue back to the empty desk.
apocalypse: A landscape of stepped cliffs made of giant filing drawers rises in terraces toward a hazy horizon, each drawer open like a ledge and spilling weathered folders down the slopes. The frosted wall panel stands as a cracked cliff face at the centre, and the hatch in it, now a doorway-sized opening, is jammed shut and silted with paper dust. A line of old office chairs has become a row of bleached frames half buried along a ledge that leads to it. A slim graphite hinge rig on thin legs is fitted to the hatch frame, and its lime arm has just swung the door open again, a thin fall of dust sliding from the sill.

title: Dinner-table buzz
hero: phone face-down beside a dinner plate
start: A small round dinner table of matte graphite sits on a pale neutral tabletop, set for two. Each place has a frosted glass plate with a neat serving of ivory card food shapes, a folded ivory napkin and slim graphite cutlery. Two sandblasted frosted glass tumblers stand between them. Beside the near plate lies a slim graphite phone slab face-down, with a thin acid-lime notification strip along its edge, dark for now. The chair opposite has a jacket over its back. A frosted acrylic candle glows softly at the centre. Fine crumbs and faint fibres rest on the napkins.
end: The same table during a flood of work. The phone is buzzing, frozen mid-jump a finger's width above the table, its acid-lime strip lit along the whole edge. The vibration has walked it across the setting: it has knocked the near tumbler, which is mid-topple with water arcing out. Ivory memo cards have spread from under the phone across both plates, covering the food, and more are frozen falling onto the table. The food shapes have gone flat and grey-edged. The chair opposite is pushed back and empty, its jacket gone. The candle has guttered and leans in its holder. Crumbs and card dust scatter outward from the phone.
apocalypse: A wide tidal flat of wet grey-ivory sediment stretches to a low, misty horizon, streaked with channels of milky water. Rising from it is the dinner table at the size of a plaza, tilted, its graphite top cracked across, both plates broken and filled with silt, and the tumblers lying on their sides like fallen towers. Memo cards have hardened into flat terraces of sediment around the ruin. The phone lies half sunk near the edge like a dark slab. A slim graphite rig on long wading legs has re-laid one clean place setting on a leveled section of the table, and its arm is drawing a lime cloth over the phone.

title: Dial-up handshake
hero: boxy modem on a desk with a phone line
start: A boxy modem about the size of a paperback sits on a small graphite desk on a pale neutral tabletop. Its case is ivory card over a graphite chassis, with a row of small frosted acrylic indicator lights across the front, one of them an acid-lime carrier light, dark and waiting. A single graphite phone line runs from its back in a neat gentle curve to a wall socket on a frosted glass panel. To the left, a graphite desk phone sits in its cradle; to the right, a cold mug and a small stack of ivory paper. Fine dust rests on the modem's vents.
end: The same modem is caught mid-retry. It has jolted a few millimetres off the desk from its own rattling, its frosted indicator lights flaring in a stuttering row, and the acid-lime carrier light is caught half lit, flickering. The phone line has whipped out of the wall socket and hangs mid-air in a loose loop, its plug swinging. The desk phone's handset has bounced out of its cradle and is mid-fall toward the floor. The paper stack beside the mug has fanned outward from the vibration, sheets sliding off the desk. Dust shakes from the vents in a thin cloud, and the socket plate is cracked.
apocalypse: A dusty scrubland of pale grey paper soil stretches toward low hills, crossed by a line of fallen graphite poles lying in the dust. At the centre, the modem sits half buried at the size of a warehouse, its ivory casing peeled and weathered, frosted lights cracked and dark. Its old phone line snakes across the plain toward the ruined frosted panel of the wall socket, but it is snapped in several places. A slim graphite cable-laying rig on thin wheels has been unspooling a new lime cable from a drum on its back, and it has just clicked the plug into the rebuilt socket, one link made.

title: Forecast board
hero: weather map board on a graphite easel
start: A weather map board about the size of a tea tray stands on a brushed graphite easel at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop. The map is ivory card with raised contour lines and softly embossed coastlines, with small graphite pressure-symbol pins placed across it. A single acid-lime front line, a thin raised strip, curves across the map. Above the easel on a slim graphite shelf, a frosted glass jar of small beads and a stack of ivory paper sit squared. A cold mug and a graphite pointer rest on a stool beside the board. Dust lies faint on the easel feet.
end: The forecast was wrong. A gust has blasted through the scene from the left, knocking the frosted glass jar off the shelf; it is mid-fall, spilling a hail of frosted beads that strike the board in a spray. The paper stack has lifted and sheets are slapping into the map. The acid-lime front line has torn half free and curls away from the card. Pressure pins have popped loose and fly outward. The easel has tipped back on two legs, and the stool is knocked over, the mug mid-roll across the tabletop. Beads bounce everywhere, all tracing back to the broken jar.
apocalypse: A storm-battered coastal headland of layered ivory card rock juts into a grey sea of frosted glass beads under a heavy sky. On the headland, the easel stands at the size of a lighthouse frame, legs bent and one snapped, with the map board torn and split, its contour lines bleached and its pins broken off. Drifts of beads have packed against the cliff and scattered across the rock. A slim graphite mast rig has bolted a new section of frame to the top of the easel, and on it a lime weather vane turns, now pointing steady into the wind.

title: Synergy merger
hero: two office models with org-chart blocks
start: Two small office building models stand side by side on a pale neutral tabletop, each about the height of a coffee cup. The left is brushed graphite, the right frosted acrylic, and both have a flat roof where a tidy org chart of ivory card blocks stands in stacked tiers, joined by thin graphite rods. The left chart is capped by a single acid-lime block at its peak. Between the buildings is a narrow gap. In the foreground, a folded ivory merger memo rests squared beside a graphite desk stamp. Dust lies faint along the roof edges.
end: The two buildings have been shoved together until their walls grind and the gap is gone. Their roof charts have merged in a crush: tiers overlap, rods snap, and duplicate ivory blocks are ejected, frozen mid-flight off both sides and tumbling toward the table. The acid-lime capstone has been knocked sideways and teeters on a jumbled pile of blocks. The frosted acrylic facade is cracked where the buildings meet. The merger memo has been scattered by falling blocks, and the stamp has tipped over. Dust spurts from the seam in a thin plume.
apocalypse: A long fault ridge crosses a wide pale plain where two landmasses have been pushed together, their edges buckled upward into a broken crest. On the crest stand the two office buildings fused at vast scale, graphite and frosted acrylic jammed together and cracked along the seam. Ejected org blocks lie scattered down both slopes like fallen boulders, weathered and bleached. A slim graphite alignment frame with lime rails stands on the crest and has stacked one clean column of blocks inside it, each block squared on the one below, rebuilding one chart.
